stem: A 10-year-old with acute asthma has an SpO2 of 92% on room air. According to the tutorial's doctor's notes, is supplemental oxygen indicated?

options.text: Yes. For children, give O2 if SpO2 is less than 95%
options.why: The doctor's notes say: give O2 if SpO2 is less than 92% (adults) or 95% (children). 92% is below the children's threshold.

options.text: No. 92% is not below the 92% threshold
options.why: 92% is the adult threshold; for children the threshold is 95%.

options.text: No. Oxygen is only needed once SpO2 is below 90%
options.why: Below 90% is one of the life-threatening findings in the Handbook figure, not the threshold for starting oxygen.

options.text: Only if the child becomes drowsy
options.why: Drowsiness is a life-threatening finding in the Handbook figure, but oxygen is already indicated by the SpO2.

explanation: Findings (child, SpO2 92% on room air) → interpretation (below the paediatric threshold of 95%) → action (give O2).

stem: A 10-year-old with acute asthma is alert, has increased work of breathing with intercostal recession, and has an SpO2 of 92%. Using the Australian Asthma Handbook categories shown in the tutorial, how severe is this attack?

options.why: Severe = any of: unable to speak in sentences, visibly breathless, increased work of breathing, oxygen saturation 90–94%.
Mild/moderate means the person can walk and speak whole sentences in one breath (young children: can move about and speak in phrases). Increased work of breathing and SpO2 90–94% are severe features.
Life-threatening = any of: drowsy, collapsed, exhausted, cyanotic, poor respiratory effort, oxygen saturation less than 90%. This child is alert with SpO2 92%.

options.text: It cannot be classified without a peak flow reading
options.why: The Handbook categories use clinical findings and oxygen saturation. Peak flow is not one of the criteria.

explanation: For severe asthma the flowchart says to start oxygen, titrating to a target saturation of at least 95% (children), and to reassess severity within minutes.

stem: Which finding classifies an acute asthma attack as life-threatening in the Handbook figures shown in the tutorial?

options.text: The person is drowsy or exhausted
options.why: Drowsy, collapsed, exhausted, cyanotic, poor respiratory effort, soft/absent breath sounds and oxygen saturation below 90% are the life-threatening findings.
Wheeze is not on the life-threatening list. Soft or absent breath sounds are.

options.text: Unable to speak in whole sentences
options.why: Being unable to speak in sentences is a severe feature, not life-threatening.
Oxygen saturation 90–94% is in the severe category; life-threatening is below 90%.

explanation: For life-threatening asthma: salbutamol by continuous nebulisation with oxygen driving the nebuliser, arrange immediate transfer to higher-level care, and notify senior staff.

stem: In life-threatening acute asthma, what gas does the Handbook figure say to use to drive the salbutamol nebuliser?

options.text: Oxygen (piped, or a cylinder with a high-flow regulator)
options.why: The figure says 'Use oxygen to drive nebuliser', with 'piped oxygen or oxygen cylinder fitted with a high-flow regulator'.

options.text: Medical air, to avoid giving too much oxygen
options.why: The figure specifies oxygen to drive the nebuliser.

options.text: No gas: give salbutamol by pMDI and spacer instead
options.why: Life-threatening asthma calls for continuous nebulisation. A pMDI with spacer is considered once breathing difficulty improves.

options.text: Room air via a face mask
options.why: The figure specifies oxygen.

explanation: This links SLO3 (oxygen) and SLO4 (inhaled medicines), and it matters for the nebuliser skill in Part B.

stem: In the Handbook figure, what flow rate is stated for the high-flow regulator used to drive the nebuliser?

options.why: The figure's footnote reads: 'Piped oxygen or oxygen cylinder fitted with a high-flow regulator (6 L/min)'.
Not the flow stated in the figure's footnote.
Not the flow stated in the figure's footnote.
Not the flow stated in the figure's footnote.

explanation: Check this against your 93225 lab guide, which may give its own nebuliser flow instruction.

stem: A patient with acute asthma on the ward is breathless again 40 minutes after their last salbutamol dose. What do the tutorial's doctor's notes direct?

options.text: Salbutamol is given only hourly on the ward; if more is needed, arrange an ICU review
options.why: The notes say 'Only administer salbutamol hourly on ward' and 'If more needed -> ICU review'.

options.text: Give up to 6 more puffs now and recheck in an hour
options.why: Up to 6 puffs is the dose, but on the ward it is given only hourly. Needing it sooner triggers an ICU review.

options.text: Wait until the next scheduled dose and do nothing else
options.why: Needing salbutamol more often than hourly triggers an ICU review, not waiting.

options.text: Give magnesium sulfate straight away instead of escalating
options.why: The notes say MgSO4 'may be given if poor response to initial management', but the stated direction when more salbutamol is needed on the ward is ICU review.

explanation: Findings (needs salbutamol sooner than hourly) → interpretation (not responding to ward-level treatment) → action (escalate for ICU review).

stem: According to the doctor's notes, how long should a patient be observed after respiratory distress has resolved?

options.why: The notes say: 'Observe patient for at least 3 hours after respiratory distress has resolved'.
One hour is when the Handbook flowchart says to reassess response to treatment. Observation after resolution is at least 3 hours.
Not the period in the doctor's notes.

options.text: No observation is needed once distress resolves
options.why: The notes set a minimum observation period of 3 hours.

explanation: At 1 hour after starting the bronchodilator, the flowchart says to reassess response: spirometry if the child is capable, and repeat pulse oximetry.

stem: Why does the tutorial say symptom monitoring can be more reliable than peak expiratory flow (PEF) for asthma self-monitoring?

options.text: Symptoms often deteriorate before PEF does
options.why: The slide states: 'Symptoms often deteriorate before PEF, therefore symptom monitoring can be more reliable than PEF'.

options.text: PEF meters are not available in Australia
options.why: The slide does not say this.
The slide's reason is the timing of deterioration.

options.text: Symptoms never change during an exacerbation
options.why: The point is that symptoms change early.

explanation: The Asthma Foundation NSW symptom diary on the slide records daytime and night-time cough/wheeze, shortness of breath, and reliever and preventer doses.

stem: On the National Asthma Council medications chart, how is montelukast classified?

options.why: Montelukast is listed under 'Non steroidal preventer' as a tablet.
The SABA relievers on the chart are salbutamol (Ventolin, Airomir) and terbutaline (Bricanyl).
ICS preventers on the chart include fluticasone, budesonide, beclometasone and ciclesonide.
The SAMA on the chart is ipratropium (Atrovent).

explanation: Other classes on the chart: LAMA, LABA, ICS-LABA, LAMA-LABA and ICS-LAMA-LABA combinations, plus biologic therapies for severe asthma.

stem: Ipratropium (Atrovent) is classified on the NAC chart as a:

options.why: Atrovent (ipratropium) is listed under 'SAMA medication'.
The SABAs on the chart are salbutamol and terbutaline.
The LABAs on the chart are formoterol, salmeterol and indacaterol.
Ipratropium is listed as a SAMA, not with the ICS preventers.

explanation: The doctor's notes add that ipratropium may be used for children with asthma, and the Handbook figures add it to nebulised salbutamol in severe and life-threatening asthma.

stem: According to the NAC chart in the tutorial, how should a pMDI (such as a salbutamol reliever) be used?

options.text: With a spacer (and a face mask if needed)
options.why: The chart states: 'pMDIs should be used with a spacer (and face mask if needed)'.
The chart says to use a spacer. The Handbook figures reserve nebulisation for severe or life-threatening attacks.

options.text: Without a spacer, to get the full dose
options.why: The chart advises a spacer.

options.text: Through a face mask without a spacer
options.why: The chart says a spacer, with a face mask added only if needed.

explanation: Inhaler technique is part of the 'education and skills' component of asthma management.

stem: Which is a LONG-TERM problem of asthma listed in the tutorial (rather than a short-term/acute one)?

options.why: School absenteeism is on the long-term list, with recurrent exacerbations, reduced lung function, activity intolerance, sleep disturbance and fatigue, and impaired growth and development.
Impaired gas exchange is on the short-term/acute list.
Anxiety/distress is on the short-term/acute list.
Breathlessness is on the short-term/acute list.

explanation: Person-centred care (SLO1) looks past the acute episode to growth, schooling and family impact.

stem: In the Clinical Reasoning Cycle used in the tutorial, which phase comes directly after 'Process information'?

options.why: The cycle runs: notice → collect cues/information → process information → identify priority needs and concerns → establish goals → take action → evaluate → reflect.
Take action comes after identifying priority needs and establishing goals.
Collecting cues comes before processing information.
Evaluation comes after action.

explanation: In 'Identify priority needs and concerns' you synthesise facts and inferences to form a nursing diagnosis.

stem: An acute asthma attack responds poorly to initial bronchodilator treatment. Which add-on treatment do the tutorial and Handbook figures name?

options.why: The doctor's notes say MgSO4 may be given for poor response, and the flowchart says 'If poor response, add IV magnesium sulfate'.
Montelukast is a non-steroidal preventer on the NAC chart, not an acute add-on in the flowcharts.
The flowcharts continue the bronchodilator and add treatment.
Antibiotics are not in the acute asthma flowcharts.

explanation: Within the first hour the flowchart also starts systemic corticosteroids, then reassesses response 1 hour after starting the bronchodilator.

prompt: Before discharge, a parent asks what to do if their child's asthma gets worse again at home. Using the tutorial's content on asthma management and written action plans, outline the education you would give.
model: Explain that asthma management aims for good symptom control (normal activity) and to minimise the risk of future attacks, fixed airflow limitation and medication side effects. Give and explain a written asthma action plan: it is personalised, helps detect and treat an exacerbation early, and states when to increase treatment, how to increase it, how long to stay on the increased treatment, and when to seek urgent medical assessment; it depends on patient and family engagement. Teach inhaler technique (pMDI with a spacer, and a face mask if needed), stress adherence, avoiding triggers and self-monitoring of symptoms (symptoms often worsen before PEF), and arrange regular review (every 6 months).

rubric.point: Written asthma action plan: early detection and personalised self-management
Action plan says when and how to increase treatment, for how long, and when to seek urgent medical assessment
Inhaler technique: pMDI with spacer (face mask if needed)
Adherence, avoiding triggers, self-monitoring of symptoms

prompt: A parent asks whether their child really needs daily preventer medication now that the child is much better. Using the tutorial's goals of asthma management, outline how you would respond.
model: Acknowledge the parent's concern and involve the family in decisions. Explain that asthma management has two goals: symptom control (good symptom control, normal activity) and risk reduction (minimising the risk of lung attacks, fixed airflow limitation and medication adverse effects). Feeling better now does not remove the risk of future attacks. Taking medicines as prescribed (adherence), inhaler technique and a written action plan are part of management, with regular review every 6 months.

rubric.point: Acknowledges the concern and involves the patient and family
Goal 1: symptom control and normal activity
Goal 2: risk reduction (lung attacks, fixed airflow limitation, medication adverse effects)
Adherence, education and regular review are core parts of management

prompt: Name the eight phases of the Clinical Reasoning Cycle, in order.
model: 1. Notice the person's current situation. 2. Collect cues/information (review, gather, recall). 3. Process information (analyse, discriminate, relate, infer, match, predict). 4. Identify priority needs and concerns (nursing diagnosis). 5. Establish goals. 6. Take action. 7. Evaluate. 8. Reflect.

rubric.point: Identify priority needs and concerns → Establish goals

stem: A child with acute asthma becomes drowsy with soft breath sounds. Continuous nebulised salbutamol driven by oxygen has been started. Apart from treatment, what does the Handbook figure direct?

options.text: Arrange immediate transfer to a higher-level care area and notify senior staff
options.why: The life-threatening pathway says 'Arrange immediate transfer to higher-level care area, notify senior staff'.
The figure says to 'Reassess immediately after starting salbutamol'.

options.text: Switch to a pMDI and spacer so the child can go home
options.why: A pMDI with spacer is considered when breathing improves; this child is deteriorating.

options.text: Stop oxygen once the nebuliser finishes
options.why: The figure says to maintain SaO2 of at least 95% in children, so oxygen continues.

explanation: Drowsy and soft/absent breath sounds are life-threatening findings. Treatment and escalation happen together.
